A divot is a small chunk of earth — grass, soil, and roots all stuck together — that gets scooped or torn out of the ground, leaving a little hollow behind. Think of it as a bite taken out of the ground.

The word actually carries two related meanings at once, and this is important:

  • The piece of turf that was removed → that's a divot.
  • The hole or depression left behind after the piece is gone → that's also called a divot.

Both meanings are correct and widely used. Context usually makes clear which one is meant.
Where You'll Hear It Most: Golf

The word is most at home on a golf course, and understanding golf makes the word click instantly.

When a golfer swings a club to hit the ball, the club's sharp edge sometimes digs into the turf and slices out a small, flat flap of grass and dirt. That flap — and the dent it leaves in the ground — is a divot.

Good golf etiquette requires players to "replace their divot," meaning they pick up that torn-out piece and press it back into the hole so the course stays smooth for others. You'll often see golfers carrying a small tool called a "divot repair tool" for this exact purpose.

So on a golf course:

  • "He took a big divot with that iron shot." → His club dug out a noticeable chunk of turf.
  • "The ball rolled right into a divot." → The ball landed in one of those little hollows in the ground.
  • "Please replace your divots." → A polite reminder on course signs.

The word has traveled well beyond golf. In everyday language, a divot refers to any small dent, hollow, or indentation in a surface — not just grass. The logic is the same: something is missing from a surface, leaving a little depression.

Examples:

  • "There's a divot in the drywall where the doorknob hit it." → A small dent in the wall.
  • "The car has a divot on the hood from the hailstorm." → A small rounded dent.
  • "The mattress has a divot in the middle from years of use." → A sunken, worn-down area.
  • "She had a small divot on her chin — a little natural indentation." → A slight hollow in skin.

In all these cases, the image is consistent: a small, localized depression where the surface dips inward or where material is missing.
The Key Qualities of a Divot

To use the word accurately, keep these features in mind:

  • Small in size. A divot is never a large crater or a wide ditch. It's modest — a few inches at most. If the hole is large, people reach for different words (pit, crater, trench, pothole).
  • Relatively shallow. A divot is a surface-level scoop, not a deep hole.
  • Caused by force or pressure. Divots don't form on their own — something digs, hits, or presses into the surface to create one.
  • Localized. A divot is a specific spot, not a general unevenness.

If you had to carry just one image in your head for "divot," let it be this: a golf club swinging down, slicing a little flap of turf out of the green, and leaving a shallow scooped-out hollow in the ground. That image — the missing piece and the depression it leaves — is the heart of the word. Everything else is just that same idea applied to walls, car hoods, mattresses, skin, or any other surface where a small chunk is missing or pushed in.
